species.description: Clownfish live inside sea anemones, whose stinging tentacles keep predators away. A coat of mucus protects the fish from the stings. Every clownfish is born male; the largest in a group becomes the female.

facts.hides: Among the tentacles of its host anemone

species.description: Adults wear bold yellow and blue stripes, while young ones are dark blue with white rings, so different they were once thought to be another species. They pick at sponges and algae on coral heads and can make a loud knocking sound when startled.

facts.hides: Ledges and caves near rich coral

species.description: Green turtles are named for the green fat under their shell, coloured by the seagrass and algae they eat. They can rest underwater for hours and return to the beach where they hatched to lay their own eggs.

facts.hides: Rests under ledges and on sand between coral

species.description: One of the largest reef fish, with a bump on its forehead that grows with age. It is one of the few animals that eats crown-of-thorns starfish, which damage coral. It is endangered because of overfishing.

facts.hides: Sleeps in caves and under ledges on the reef slope

species.description: Tuskfish have strong, forward-pointing teeth that look like little tusks. They turn over rubble and sand to find crabs, clams and sea urchins, sometimes smashing shells on rocks.

facts.hides: Sand and rubble near seagrass and coral

species.description: Unlike most octopuses, this one hunts by day. It can change colour and skin texture in a fraction of a second to match the coral, and carries its den's entrance tidy by pushing out shells.

facts.length: Body about 16 cm; arms reach about 80 cm
facts.hides: A den in a rock crack, often marked by a pile of shells

species.description: Unlike many sharks, the whitetip can lie still on the sand and pump water over its gills. It rests in caves by day and hunts fish in coral cracks at night. It is shy and rarely a danger to people.

facts.length: Up to 2.1 m, usually under 1.6 m
facts.hides: Rests on sand or in caves during the day

species.description: Powder blue tangs graze algae from rocks and coral, often in groups that move together across the reef. Like all surgeonfish, they have a sharp spine near the tail they can use in defence.

facts.length: Up to 54 cm, usually around 23 cm
facts.hides: Shallow reef flats and upper slopes
